1555.dq: Such patterning is not consistent, of course, but it is common enough to confuse any learner who expects to find stresses observed in isolated words to be preserved in the context of a sentence.
1555.dloc: Benton 1971, Phonology: 'Stress' and 'Stress contrasts', pp. 24-26 (also 'Shift in stress' p. 87); Rubino 2001 p. 539-540
1555.prule: Primary ('strong') stress is lexically contrastive on the root (penult vs. final minimal pairs: láki/lakí, bálo/baló, etc.); no positional or weight rule for the strong stress is given. Stressed open-syllable vowels lengthen (Rubino).
1555.srule: Secondary ('moderate/medium') stress, stated as tendencies: (i) every closed syllable automatically attracts a moderate stress (nátàn 'now'); (ii) every alternate syllable preceding or following the lexical strong stress tends to attract medium stress (kàbuasán 'morning', mansásalìta 'is speaking'); the two tendencies may neutralize each other (pànggasinán).

1556.prule: Penultimate stress by default; stress shifts to the final syllable when the word ends in a consonant (final closed = heavy syllable). Lexical exceptions exist and are marked with a written accent in the orthography (exceptional final stress on light-final words; a dozen words with antepenultimate stress).
1556.srule: Secondary (rhythmic) stress is quantity-insensitive and strictly binary, never on a syllable adjacent to the primary stress (no clash). Which of two patterns a word takes is a lexical property of its root: 'regular' (about 66% of relevant words in Parker's corpus) on odd-numbered syllables counting from the beginning of the word (left-to-right syllabic trochees); 'irregular' (about 34%) on even-numbered syllables from the beginning of the word, i.e. iterating leftward from the primary stress. Trisyllables with final primary stress are attested with a single stress (Bennett 2013: 371; Parker p.c. there disagrees).

tn.quote: There are four contrastive tonemes in Pa-O language spoken at Huay Salop village, three contour tones: high rising, high falling, and low falling, and one level tone: mid level. 1559.dq: In this section, we will lay out the main facts in relation to the word-level stress pattern of Curaçao Papiamentu, on the basis of the data in Kouwenberg & Murray (1994) and Kouwenberg (2004).
1559.heavy: closed syllables counting as heavy (non-verbs only; hedged 'to some extent predictable', 'many exceptions')
1559.dflt: penultimate (non-verbs); verbs: penult in disyllabic base forms, final in participles and in longer verbs
1559.prule: Lexically distinctive word stress (final/penult/antepenult all occur; minimal pairs e.g. 'lora 'to turn' vs lo'ra 'turned'). Sub-regularities: verbs - disyllabic base forms penultimate, participles final (stress shift = participle morphology), longer verbs final; non-verbs - penultimate unless the final syllable is closed (heavy), then final, 'with many exceptions' that follow the lexifier (Spanish/Portuguese/Dutch) stress. Independent word-level tone contrast (Tone I vs Tone II).
1559.srule: Secondary stress on alternating syllables preceding or following the primary stress, predictable from the position of the primary (e.g. 'agui`la, `ombe'skop, `kumin'sa); the secondary on the final syllable of antepenult-stressed words is confirmed acoustically (longer vowel, no F0 mark).
1559.quote: Curaçao Papiamentu has both lexically distinctive stress and, independently, a word-level tone contrast. ... In verbs, the location of primary stress is predictable from the number of syllables and the morphological category. The vast majority of disyllabic verbs have penultimate stress in the base form. ... In the corresponding participle forms (1b), however, stress is on the final syllable. ... Longer verbs uniformly have final stress, both in the base form and in the participle ... In nouns, adjectives and adverbs – i.e. in all lexical categories other than verbs – stress is to some extent…
1559.idn: Curaçao dialect of Papiamentu (Curaçao Papiamentu); data: Stress description 'on the basis of the data in Kouwenberg & Murray (1994) and Kouwenberg (2004)' (§2.2.1 p. 207). Own acoustic data: 'The recordings were made in Willemstad, Curaçao, in the offices of the Fundashon pa Planifikashon di Idioma (FPI)'…
1559.exq_: However, there are many exceptions to this weight-sensitive stress rule – see the examples in (3). In these examples, stress tends to follow the stress pattern of the word in the relevant lexifier language, resulting in irregular final, penultimate and antepenultimate stress patterns.
1559.tone: Independent binary word-level tone contrast (Tone I vs Tone II; Joubert 1991 lists 251 tone-only minimal pairs, e.g. Tone I 'lora 'parrot' vs Tone II 'lora 'to turn'); authors propose a privative (Scandinavian-accent-like) analysis. Tone is independent of stress position, so this is not a tone or pitch accent-only system: stress is separately contrastive.

tn.quote: In addition to word-level stress, Curaçao Papiamentu has a word-level tone distinction. ... The majority of words have rising pitch on the stressed syllable in the citation form ... Most disyllabic verbs, however, have falling pitch on the penultimate syllable and rising pitch on the final syllable in the same contexts. ... Hereafter we will refer to these tone patterns as TONE I and TONE II, respectively. ... We hypothesise that tone II involves a lexical tone, but that tone I does not. In other words, the Curaçao Papiamentu tone contrast is accounted for in terms of a privative lexical tone.

1561.prule: Accent is anchored to morphemes, not to word syllable count: the ROOT carries accent on its final syllable (roots mostly monosyllabic; the rare disyllabic roots are accented on the last syllable, regardless of vowel quality, Araújo 1993:267); PREFIXES are never accented and leave root accent untouched; SUFFIXES are normally accented as well (unless their vowel is reduced) and also leave the root accent untouched, so suffixed words carry two successive accented syllables with the clash maintained (küm'xê're, ka'xê're) and no primary/secondary ranking stated. In compounds each member keeps its own accent. quantity-insensitive; orthography leaves accent unmarked as predictable (Araújo 2016 apud Quaresma: 'sempre na segunda sílaba' = second syllable of a disyllabic root).
1561.srule: No ranked secondary stress and no rhythmic stress described. The source states an additional word accent placed by morphology: full-vowel suffixes are accented next to the root-final accent, so a suffixed word has two successive accented syllables (küm'xê're 'bacuri', ka'xê're 'étoile'), the clash kept with neither accent displaced or reduced; which of the two is the main accent is not stated (prefixes are never accented).

1565.prule: Mora-counting metrical stress: final syllable extrametrical; morae parsed left-to-right into iambic (μ μ́) feet; primary stress on the last foot of the word (sometimes the last foot of the stem), i.e. Table 3.18: odd mora count -> stress on the penultimate mora, even mora count -> on the antepenultimate mora. 1573.dq: The phonological word is a stress group that may consist of one to six or more syllables. Stress occurs on one or more syllables and is of two types, high stress /V́/, marked by high pitch, and low stress /V̀/, marked by low pitch. ... Each word has at least one stressed syllable, but may have more.

1573.prule: Stress placement is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs by position, e.g. íimaca 'he said' vs iimáca 'he slept'); no fixed position and no weight rule. Stress also contrasts in quality: 'high stress' (high pitch) vs 'low stress' (low pitch). A word has 1 to 5 stresses; only restriction: stress never falls on the second of two identical vowels in sequence. Morphophonemic stress shifts at V+V morpheme junctures and 'prestressed' suffixes (sec. 2.5) that place stress on the preceding vowel.
1573.srule: No primary/secondary ranking is set up: a word carries one to five stresses, each lexically (morphemically) placed, of two contrastive kinds, high stress (high pitch, 'somewhat heavier') and low stress (low pitch); several of either kind may occur in one word, also on contiguous syllables; 'prestressed' suffixes (e.g. gerund -V́ná) add a high stress to the preceding stem vowel. No rhythmic or alternating stress is described.

1573.tone: Stress is realized by pitch: 'high stress, marked by high tone V́' vs 'low stress, marked by low tone V̀', both contrastive (nuyáaca 'I ate' vs nuyàaca 'I wove'); unstressed syllables 'tend to rise or fall in pitch according to their proximity to stressed syllables'. 1575.srule: Secondary ('medial') stress is a third contrastive stress phoneme: every polysyllabic word's superfix has one primary stress plus 'one or more medial or weak stresses', and which non-primary syllables are medial rather than weak is part of the contrastive word superfix (lexically/morphemically specified), e.g. /píwene/ 'rabbit' (primary-weak-weak) vs /pìwénę̀/ 'rabbits' (medial-primary-medial); no positional or alternating rule; a primary stress reduces to medial or weak when syllables combine.

1576.prule: Primary stress generally, 'but by no means exclusively', on the penultimate syllable of the word (Grant 2013 sec. 5, the only placement statement in either cited work). In the dominant disyllabic vocabulary penult = initial (náyka, yáka, máyka, wáwa, íkta, tílxam, páłač, skúkum, łátwa, mámuk, úkuk, čáku), with final-stressed exceptions in the chapter's own forms (sayá 'far', kəním 'canoe', hayú 'many', yakwá, and French-origin nouns with incorporated article such as latáb 'table'). For words of three or more syllables the chapter's accent-marked forms are mostly initial rather than penult (ánqati, tílixam 'person', íli’i, támulič 'barrel', sínamakwst 'seven', kálakala 'bird', ták’umunaq 'hundred'; penult only nawítka 'certainly'; final kʰanawí 'all'), so the stated penult default is secure only where it coincides with initial stress. Hale 1890 states no positional rule: accent 'cannot be known from the orthography' and is marked per dictionary entry with an acute. Vowel lengthening ('stress of the voice': hyas, ahnkottie; sayáaa) is expressive emphasis, not lexical contrast. No secondary stress described.

1579.prule: Main stress on the final syllable if it contains a long vowel, otherwise on the penultimate syllable (equivalently: penultimate vowel/mora if long vowels are counted as VV). Secondary stress on alternate syllables leftward from the antepenult, modulo morphological structure.
1579.srule: Secondary stress on alternate syllables counting back from the antepenultimate, i.e. every second syllable leftward from the main stress (malamake [ˌmalaˈmake]); in morphologically complex words lexical roots and some affixes keep their own stress, which can override the count (hakamemea [ˌhakameˈmea] = haka- + memea).
